questions.stem: What does an infrared spectrophotometer measure?

options.text: The intensity of infrared radiation transmitted through the sample at each wavelength
options.explanation: The instrument sweeps the infrared range and records which frequencies the sample absorbs by their missing intensity.

options.text: The mass-to-charge ratio of molecular fragments
options.explanation: That is the mass spectrometer's job, not the infrared one.

options.text: The boiling point range of the liquid sample
options.explanation: Boiling behaviour belongs to purity testing, not infrared analysis.

options.text: The colour changes of an indicator during titration
options.explanation: That belongs to acid-base titrations.

questions.stem: Bonds respond to absorbed infrared radiation by

options.text: Combining with neighbouring molecules
options.explanation: Absorption does not create new bonds between molecules.

options.text: Stretching, bending and twisting more vigorously at their own resonance frequency
options.explanation: Each bond has a specific frequency that enlarges its natural vibration when matched.

options.text: Breaking permanently into radicals
options.explanation: Absorption excites vibrations; it does not normally snap the bond.

options.text: Losing their electrons to the detector
options.explanation: Infrared absorption moves vibrational energy, not electron removal.

questions.stem: The wavenumber recorded on an infrared spectrum is

options.text: The frequency in hertz divided by the speed of light squared
options.explanation: That expression does not define wavenumber.

options.text: The time taken for one vibration cycle
options.explanation: That is a period, the inverse of frequency, not wavenumber.

options.text: The reciprocal of the radiation's wavelength, expressed per centimetre
options.explanation: Wavenumber in cm-1 is 1 divided by the wavelength in centimetres.

options.text: The wavelength of radiation in nanometres
options.explanation: Wavenumber is the reciprocal, not the wavelength itself.

questions.stem: An O-H absorption in an alcohol spectrum is typically broad because

options.text: The O-H bond is the weakest bond in the molecule
options.explanation: Bond strength does not set bandwidth; the hydrogen-bond spread does.

options.text: The spectrometer scans that region too quickly
options.explanation: Scan speed does not broaden a real absorption band.

options.text: Alcohol samples are always impure
options.explanation: Purity is irrelevant; pure alcohols still show the broad hydrogen-bonded band.

options.text: Hydrogen bonding between molecules spreads the absorption over a range of frequencies
options.explanation: Each hydrogen-bonded environment absorbs slightly differently, smearing the band.

questions.stem: A strong, sharp absorption near 1710 wavenumbers most strongly suggests the presence of

options.text: A carbonyl C=O group
options.explanation: The polar C=O double bond gives a strong, sharp absorption in that region.

options.text: An alcohol O-H group
options.explanation: The alcohol O-H absorbs broadly around 3200-3500.

options.text: A C-C single bond in an alkane backbone
options.explanation: Backbone single bonds absorb outside the diagnostic carbonyl region and are weak.

options.text: A nitrogen-hydrogen stretch of an amine
options.explanation: N-H absorbs in the 3300 region and is not the 1710 marker.

questions.stem: Define the resonance frequency of a bond in infrared spectroscopy.
questions.modelAnswer: The resonance frequency is the specific radiation frequency at which a bond's vibration responds most strongly, producing a recorded absorption.

questions.stem: State the typical shapes of the O-H and C=O absorbances.
questions.modelAnswer: The hydrogen-bonded O-H absorption is broad, while the carbonyl C=O absorption is strong and sharp.

questions.stem: Explain why different functional groups absorb different infrared frequencies.
questions.modelAnswer: Each bond's vibrating mass and stiffness set its own resonance frequency, so groups built from different atoms and bond orders absorb at characteristic wavenumbers that identify them.

questions.stem: An unknown liquid shows a broad absorption near 3350 wavenumbers and nothing sharp near 1710. Suggest its functional group and one structure check you would run next.
questions.modelAnswer: The broad 3350 band marks an alcohol O-H with no carbonyl present, so a mass spectrum to confirm the molecular mass would be a sensible next check before naming the compound.

questions.stem: Why can an infrared spectrum alone fail to identify an unknown compound?

options.text: The table of ranges is only valid for hydrocarbons
options.explanation: The ranges cover all the common organic bonds, not just hydrocarbons.

options.text: Absorption ranges of different bonds overlap, so one peak may belong to several bond types
options.explanation: Overlapping bands make single-peak assignments ambiguous, requiring a second technique.

options.text: Infrared spectra only show impurities, never functional groups
options.explanation: Functional-group absorbances are exactly what infrared spectra show.

options.text: Wavenumbers vary with the weather in the laboratory
options.explanation: Absorption positions are molecular properties, not weather-dependent.

questions.stem: A spectrum shows a strong, sharp peak at about 1710 wavenumbers. Which compound fits best?

options.text: Hexane, which has no polar bonds at all
options.explanation: Hexane lacks a carbonyl and would not show the 1710 spike.

options.text: Water, which absorbs across a wide microwave band
options.explanation: Water's absorptions are broad and outside the carbonyl marker.

options.text: Propanone, whose ketone carbonyl absorbs there
options.explanation: The C=O of a ketone gives the strong, sharp 1710 absorption.

options.text: Propan-2-ol, whose O-H absorbs broadly at 3200-3500
options.explanation: An alcohol spectrum would show the broad hydroxyl band instead.

questions.stem: A second spectrum of the same formula shows a strong broad band from 3200 to 3500 wavenumbers. The compound is

options.text: The ketone, since all oxygen compounds share the same spectrum
options.explanation: Ketones and alcohols absorb differently despite both containing oxygen.

options.text: An alkane, since the formula is unchanged
options.explanation: Same formula does not mean same functional group or spectrum.

options.text: Impossible to decide from the infrared data
options.explanation: The broad O-H band is decisive evidence for the alcohol.

options.text: The alcohol, since a broad 3200-3500 band is the O-H signature
options.explanation: Hydrogen bonding broadens the O-H absorption, and its position marks the alcohol.

questions.stem: Which technique is named as the standard partner to infrared spectroscopy when absorption bands overlap?

options.text: Mass spectroscopy
options.explanation: Fragment and molecular-ion evidence resolves what overlapping infrared bands cannot.

options.text: Flame tests
options.explanation: Flame tests identify metal ions, not organic functional groups.

options.text: Thin-layer chromatography
options.explanation: Chromatography separates mixtures but is not the named infrared partner here.

options.text: Boiling-point determination
options.explanation: Boiling behaviour checks purity rather than resolving overlapping absorbances.

questions.stem: The absorption-range table is best used by

options.text: Using the table only for inorganic unknowns
options.explanation: The ranges serve organic functional-group identification.

options.text: Finding the observed peak position and listing every bond whose range covers it, then using peak shape to decide
options.explanation: The table narrows candidates, and width plus intensity discriminate within them.

options.text: Reading the first bond listed whose range is nearby
options.explanation: Stopping at the first match ignores overlapping candidates.

options.text: Ignoring peak shape, since position alone decides
options.explanation: Shape is precisely what separates broad O-H from sharp C=O at adjacent positions.

questions.stem: State the wavenumber regions quoted for the carbonyl C=O and the alcohol O-H absorbances.
questions.modelAnswer: The carbonyl group absorbs sharply around 1710 wavenumbers and the alcohol O-H absorbs broadly around 3200 to 3500 wavenumbers.

questions.stem: State what must be done before infrared data are used to assign an unknown compound when ranges overlap.
questions.modelAnswer: A complementary technique, mass spectroscopy, joins the infrared evidence before the structure is assigned.

questions.stem: Explain why comparing an unknown spectrum with the spectrum of a known compound is a valid identification strategy.
questions.modelAnswer: Absorption positions, widths and intensities reproduce for the same structure, so a matching pattern of absorbances between unknown and reference demonstrates the same functional groups and supports the identification.

questions.stem: Two colourless liquids, one a ketone and one an alcohol, have lost their labels. Describe the infrared evidence that restores each label and state the diagnostic wavenumber regions you would quote.
questions.modelAnswer: The ketone is the liquid whose spectrum carries a strong, sharp absorption near 1710 for its C=O group; the alcohol is the one showing the strong, broad 3200-3500 band of its hydrogen-bonded O-H group.
